## Design

### 2026-10-09 – ![Screenshot 2026-10-09 9.02.16 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/p82XWUXIJ9Qpmi5y0NjrKPd5gfPaDnPX/5ef51eee2da7417e23b43ac32a787daf0d148d2a0d64fd224063cba297ac389a.p

**3h**

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 9.02.16 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/p82XWUXIJ9Qpmi5y0NjrKPd5gfPaDnPX/5ef51eee2da7417e23b43ac32a787daf0d148d2a0d64fd224063cba297ac389a.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-09 9.02.55 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/p82XWUXIJ9Qpmi5y0NjrKPd5gfPaDnPX/1bc6b5fad6678948ad2e48cee7deb9602f9fdb85c27d2ff2e6400b2d8cee49e5.png)

Today marked the beginning of bringing Starbie to life, starting at the very foundation of any custom electronics project: designing the PCB schematic. After launching KiCad and initializing a new project file, I opened up the Schematic Editor to chart every electrical connection. The first major task was adding the main brain of the system—the XIAO-ESP32-C3 microcontroller. To establish power distribution while keeping the workspace clean and unburdened by a web of crossing wires, I laid down the +5V, +3.3V, and GND power symbols, using net labels to define implicit connections across the circuit.

With power routed, I focused on adding interactivity and environmental perception. I wired up tactile push buttons (SW_Push) connecting net lines directly to ground for physical inputs. Next came the visual and motion hardware: a 01x04 pin header to serve as the interface for Starbie's display screen, and a 01x08 pin header to represent the MPU6050 motion-sensing module so the device can detect movement. To complete the sensor suit, I integrated a DHT11 sensor symbol, giving Starbie the ability to read ambient temperature and humidity levels.

The final crucial phase was bridging schematic logic to physical manufacturing by assigning footprints to each symbol. Opening the Footprint Assignment Tool, I mapped every component to its real-world board layout—making sure to select the custom ESP32-C3 footprint imported from the Care Package. Once all pins and physical pads were aligned, I applied and saved the complete schematic, officially closing out the logic design phase and setting the stage to route the physical PCB layout.

### 2026-10-09 – With the schematic finalized, I transitioned into the KiCad PCB Editor and pulled in all our components using the "Update PCB from schematic" tool. After scattering the footprints onto the canvas, I d

**6h**

With the schematic finalized, I transitioned into the KiCad PCB Editor and pulled in all our components using the "Update PCB from schematic" tool. After scattering the footprints onto the canvas, I drew a custom board outline on the Edge.Cuts layer and carefully arranged the components within its borders. Then came routing: pressing X, I mapped out traces across both the front (F.Cu) and back (B.Cu) copper layers, following the blue ratsnest lines to join every matching golden pad. I capped off the physical layout by adding a ground plane pour across the board to ensure clean power distribution.

Before moving on to the software, I ran KiCad’s Design Rules Check (DRC) to catch any layout flaws. After resolving a couple of missing trace connections and ensuring zero critical errors remained, I used KiCad’s Image Converter tool to add custom artwork to the board's silkscreen, giving the physical hardware a distinct personality.

Next, I turned my attention to setting up Starbie's firmware inside the Arduino IDE. I added the Espressif package URL to my preferences, installed the esp32 board platform, and configured the target board to the XIAO_ESP32C3. Through the Library Manager, I grabbed all necessary hardware drivers—Adafruit GFX, Adafruit SSD1306, Adafruit MPU6050, and the DHT sensor library—before opening up Starbie.ino.

To wrap up the day, I customized Starbie’s code within the BEGINNER SETTINGS block. I mapped the GPIO pin assignments to match the exact hardware lines for the I2C display, MPU6050 sensor, DHT11, and input buttons, and tuned the four-choice radial menu actions (NAP, PLAY, FEED, PET). I then wrote a custom drawSparkle rendering function to spawn a glowing pixel trail behind Starbie as it walks across the screen, and converted a custom 32x32 pixel sprite into a byte array using image2cpp to replace PET_SPRITE, giving Starbie a completely unique look and feel.
